mainTopic: נדרי שגגות (vows made by mistake), mistaken שבועות, רבי עקיבא's rule that a partly permitted vow is fully permitted, and רבה's explanation of the figs dispute.
overview: The משנה lists cases of נדרי שגגות, vows built on a mistaken fact, which are not binding. In one case he ties a קונם to something he thinks he never did. In another he sets off his own condition by forgetting. In a third he makes a vow because of a false accusation. The משנה then brings a man who forbids his figs to a group that turns out to include his father and brother, and records a מחלוקת: בית שמאי permit only the relatives, while בית הלל permit everyone. The גמרא adds a ברייתא that mistaken שבועות are also not binding, with the example of רב כהנא and רב אסי, who each honestly swore to a different version of רב's teaching. Turning to the figs case, the גמרא quotes a משנה about opening vows using שבתות and ימים טובים, which ends with רבי עקיבא's rule that a vow partly permitted is fully permitted. Finally רבה explains the figs dispute by wording. If the man would have said 'all of you except father,' everyone agrees the others stay forbidden. בית שמאי and בית הלל argue only if he would have named each person and permitted his father separately.

steps.title: Examples of vows made by mistake
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists three kinds of נדרי שגגות: a vow tied to a past act he wrongly thought never happened, a vow whose condition he set off by forgetting, and a vow based on a false accusation.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNAH: Vows made by mistake: someone says 'This is forbidden to me if I ate or drank' and then remembers that he did eat and drink. Or he says 'This is forbidden to me if I eat or drink,' and then forgets and eats and drinks. Or he says 'My wife is forbidden to benefit from me because she stole my wallet and hit my son,' and then it turns out she did not hit him and did not steal.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה defines נדרי שגגות by giving clear examples. In each case the vow rests on a fact the person had wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case he thought he had not eaten, so he never meant the vow to take effect. In the second he forgot the condition he had set, so he set it off only by mistake and the prohibition does not take hold. In the third, the whole reason for the vow, his wife's supposed wrongdoing, was never true, so the vow has no basis.

keyTerms.meaning: Vows made by mistake, based on wrong information
A vow word: 'forbidden to me like a קרבן'

steps.whyThisMatters: These cases set the basic rule: a vow built on a false fact is not binding.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: Vows made by mistake:
'[This is forbidden to me] if I ate or if I drank,'
phrases.notes: He is sure he did not eat, so he ties the vow to something he thinks never happened.

phrases.english: and then he remembered that he had eaten and drunk.
'[This is forbidden to me] if I eat or if I drink,'
and he forgot and ate and drank.
He said: 'It is קונם for my wife to benefit from me'
because she stole my wallet
and because she hit my son,'
and it became known that she had not hit him,
and it became known that she had not stolen.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow based on a mistaken fact (past, forgotten, or false accusation) counts as a נדר שגגה and is not binding.

steps.title: The figs case: father and brother among the eaters
steps.stepSummary: A man forbids his figs to a group, then finds out his father and brother were among them. בית שמאי permit only the relatives; בית הלל permit everyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: He saw people eating figs and said: 'These are like a קרבן to you!' Then it turned out that his father and brother were there, along with other people. בית שמאי say: the father and brother are permitted, and the others with them are forbidden. בית הלל say: both groups are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה brings one more mistaken vow, where only part of the vow was a mistake, and records a מחלוקת about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He never meant to forbid his own father and brother, so that part of the vow is clearly a mistake. בית שמאי cancel only the mistaken part, so strangers stay forbidden. בית הלל say that once part of the vow falls away, the whole vow falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This is like a קרבן to you': a vow forbidding the item to them

steps.confusionAlert: בית שמאי agree the father and brother are permitted. The argument is only about the strangers who were with them.
steps.whyThisMatters: This מחלוקת raises whether a vow that is partly cancelled stays partly in force. The גמרא will tie it to רבי עקיבא's rule.

phrases.english: He saw them eating figs,
and he said: 'They are like a קרבן to you!'
and it turned out they were his father and brother,
and there were other people with them.
Beis Shammai say: they are permitted,
and those who are with them are forbidden.
And Beis Hillel say:
both these and those are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a case where only part of the vow was a mistake.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: only the father and brother are permitted. בית הלל: everyone in the group is permitted.

steps.title: Mistaken oaths are also not binding
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that mistaken שבועות are permitted, just like mistaken vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: A ברייתא taught: just as vows made by mistake are permitted, so too oaths made by mistake are permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא that takes the משנה's rule about vows and applies it to oaths too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נדר forbids an object, while a שבועה binds the person. Even so, the ברייתא says a mistake cancels a שבועה just as it cancels a נדר.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: It was taught in a ברייתא:
Just as vows made by mistake are permitted,
so too oaths made by mistake are permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the משנה's rule from vows to oaths.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oaths made by mistake are not binding, just like vows made by mistake.

steps.title: What does a mistaken oath look like?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a real example of a שבועת שגגה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a case of oaths made by mistake?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a concrete example of the ברייתא's rule. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave examples for vows but none for oaths. The גמרא wants to see a real situation where someone swears by mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What does it look like?

phrases.english: What is the case of oaths made by mistake?

steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete example of a שבועת שגגה.

steps.title: Two sages each swear about what רב said
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא and רב אסי each swore that רב held his own opinion. Each honestly believed he was right, so one of them swore falsely by mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: For example, רב כהנא and רב אסי: this one said, 'I swear that this is what רב said,' and that one said, 'I swear that this is what רב said.' Each one, in his own mind, was swearing honestly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a real story. Two sages swore opposite things about רב's teaching, and both truly believed what they said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both cannot be right, so one oath was false. But nobody lied on purpose, because each was sure of his memory. That honest mistake is exactly what a שבועת שגגה is.
steps.whatToRemember: A שבועת שגגה is an oath a person swore honestly but that turns out false, like two sages each sure they remembered רב correctly.

phrases.english: For example, Rav Kahana and Rav Asi:
this one said: 'I swear'
'that this is what Rav said,'
phrases.notes: They were arguing about a הלכה, and each claimed רב agreed with him.

phrases.english: and that one said: 'I swear'
'that this is what Rav said.'
For each and every one, according to his own mind,
was swearing properly.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A שבועת שגגה is like two sages each swearing, in good faith, to opposite versions of רב's teaching.

steps.title: Back to the figs case: quoting another משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the figs case and quotes a משנה from later in the מסכת: vows may be opened using שבתות and ימים טובים.
steps.simpleTranslation: About 'he saw them eating': we learned in a משנה elsewhere: we may open a vow using שבתות and ימים טובים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the figs case and brings in another משנה. This is a setup line that prepares the comparison to come.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone vowed not to eat something 'every day,' he can say he never meant שבת and יום טוב. That opens a door to cancel the vow. Like the figs case, part of the vow was clearly not intended.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned there, in another משנה
We 'open' a vow: find a reason to cancel it

steps.confusionAlert: 'פותחין' does not mean opening a door. It means finding an opening, a reason the person never really intended the vow, so a חכם can cancel it.

phrases.english: 'He saw them eating':
We learned there:
phrases.notes: This משנה appears later in this מסכת, on דף 66a.

phrases.english: We open [a vow] using Shabbosos and Yamim Tovim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the oath topic and returns to the figs case from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow may be opened by pointing out that the person never meant to include שבתות and ימים טובים.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: partly permitted means fully permitted
steps.stepSummary: At first, people held that only the unintended days were permitted. רבי עקיבא taught that once part of a vow is permitted, the whole vow is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: At first they used to say: those days are permitted and all the other days are forbidden. Then רבי עקיבא came and taught: a vow that was partly permitted is entirely permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The quoted משנה continues with an older view and then רבי עקיבא's rule, which replaced it. The גמרא is setting up a comparison to the figs case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The older view kept the vow alive for ordinary days and permitted only שבת and יום טוב. רבי עקיבא said a vow cannot be split, so if part falls away, all of it falls away. This sounds like בית הלל's view that strangers are permitted too.

keyTerms.meaning: The great תנא whose rule changed the earlier practice
A vow partly permitted is fully permitted

steps.whatToRemember: רבי עקיבא's rule: a vow that is partly permitted is fully permitted. Keep it in mind alongside בית הלל in the figs case.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule is a central idea in הלכות נדרים, and the גמרא will use it to understand the בית שמאי and בית הלל argument.

phrases.english: At first they used to say:
those days are permitted,
phrases.notes: 'Those days' means the שבתות and ימים טובים he never meant to include.

phrases.english: and all the other days are forbidden,
until Rabbi Akiva came and taught:
A vow that was partly permitted
is permitted entirely.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the quoted משנה, moving from the older view to רבי עקיבא's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: נדר שהותר מקצתו הותר כולו: a vow that is partly permitted is entirely permitted.

steps.title: רבה: The case where everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: רבה says that if the man would have said 'all of you are forbidden except father,' then everyone agrees: the others are forbidden and only the father is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Everyone agrees that whenever he says, 'Had I known my father was among you, I would have said: All of you are forbidden except father,' then all the others are forbidden and his father is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה starts explaining the argument in the figs case by first naming a case where there is no argument at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key is how the man says he would have worded the vow if he had known. If it would have been one sentence with an exception, 'all of you except father,' both בית שמאי and בית הלל agree. The vow stays on everyone else, and only the father is let out.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees (here, both בית שמאי and בית הלל)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי עקיבא's rule from the previous step ('part permitted, all permitted') automatically applies here. רבה says that in this wording, everyone agrees the others stay forbidden.

phrases.english: Rabba said: Everyone agrees,
phrases.notes: 'Everyone' here means both בית שמאי and בית הלל from the משנה about the figs.

phrases.english: wherever he says:
Had I known that father was among you,
I would have said: "All of you are forbidden, except father,"
then all of them are forbidden and his father is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the rule of רבי עקיבא, רבה defines which version of the figs case is not in dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If he would have said 'all of you except father,' all agree: the others are forbidden and the father is permitted.

steps.title: רבה: The case where they argue
steps.stepSummary: רבה says בית שמאי and בית הלל argue only when the man would have said 'so-and-so and so-and-so are forbidden, and father is permitted.'
steps.simpleTranslation: They argued only when he says, 'Had I known my father was among you, I would have said: So-and-so and so-and-so are forbidden, and father is permitted.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבה finishes his statement by naming the one case where בית שמאי and בית הלל really do argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the man would have named each person one by one, instead of saying 'all of you except father.' Only in this wording does the משנה's argument apply. So the dispute is now limited to this specific way of speaking.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה splits the figs case by wording. 'All of you except father' means everyone agrees the others are forbidden. 'So-and-so and so-and-so are forbidden, and father is permitted' is the only case where בית שמאי and בית הלל argue.
steps.whyThisMatters: This narrows the משנה's argument to one precise kind of wording, which shapes how the rest of the סוגיא reads the dispute.

phrases.english: They disagreed only where he says:
Had I known that father was among you,
I would have said: "So-and-so and so-and-so are forbidden
and father is permitted."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבה's statement by naming the case of dispute, in contrast to the case of agreement in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל applies only when he would have listed each person by name and permitted the father separately.
